hints: List all ions actually present in each solution, remembering that water provides $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ in addition to the ions from the salt.
At the cathode think about which positive ion is easier to reduce, a reactive metal versus hydrogen from water, using the reactivity series.
At the anode think about which negative ion is easier to oxidise, and remember that very concentrated $\text{Cl}^{-}$ can discharge in preference to $\text{OH}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Sort out who can move to each electrode**
Picture each solution with four ions. For $\text{AgNO}_{3}\text{(aq)}$ you have $\text{Ag}^{+}$ and $\text{H}^{+}$ able to go to the negative cathode, and $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ able to go to the positive anode. The same idea applies to $\text{Na}^{+}$, $\text{H}^{+}$, $\text{Cl}^{-}$, $\text{OH}^{-}$ in brine, and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, $\text{H}^{+}$, $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$, $\text{OH}^{-}$ in copper sulfate.

Decide the cathode product**
Silver and copper are both well below sodium and hydrogen in reactivity, so $\text{Ag}^{+}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ pick up electrons very easily to give metal: $\text{Ag}^{+}+\text{e}^{-}\rightarrow\text{Ag}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}+2\text{e}^{-}\rightarrow\text{Cu}$. Sodium is far too reactive to be discharged from water, so in concentrated $\text{NaCl(aq)}$ it is $\text{H}^{+}$ from water that is reduced: $2\text{H}^{+}+2\text{e}^{-}\rightarrow\text{H}_{2}$.

Decide the anode product**
$\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ are very stable and stay in solution, so $\text{OH}^{-}$ is oxidised to oxygen: $4\text{OH}^{-}\rightarrow\text{O}_{2}+2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}+4\text{e}^{-}$. In concentrated chloride solution the large concentration of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ allows chloride to discharge instead: $2\text{Cl}^{-}\rightarrow\text{Cl}_{2}+2\text{e}^{-}$, even though dilute brine would give oxygen.

Final answer: $\text{AgNO}_{3}\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_{2}$, cathode $\text{Ag}$
concentrated $\text{NaCl(aq)}$: anode $\text{Cl}_{2}$, cathode $\text{H}_{2}$
$\text{CuSO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_{2}$, cathode $\text{Cu}$

hints: Recall that molten $\text{CaI}_{2}$ contains only $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$, so there is no competition from water.
Remember oxidation (loss of electrons) happens at the anode and reduction (gain of electrons) happens at the cathode, and balance charge with electrons.
walkthrough:
See why the melt is simple**
When $\text{CaI}_{2}$ is molten there is no water at all. The only ions free to move are $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ toward the cathode and $\text{I}^{-}$ toward the anode. That makes the electrode reactions very clean.

Write the two half-equations**
At the positive anode, negative iodide ions lose electrons: $2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow \text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$. At the negative cathode, positive calcium ions gain the electrons: $\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ca}$. Both are balanced for atoms and for charge.

hints: Link each half-equation from (b)(i) to loss or gain of electrons to identify which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
Assign the oxidation number of $\text{Ca}$ and $\text{I}$ before and after reaction, using the rules for simple ions and free elements.
walkthrough:
Use electrons to spot redox**
Iodide loses electrons to form iodine, and loss of electrons is oxidation. Calcium ion gains electrons to form calcium metal, and gain of electrons is reduction. Because oxidation and reduction happen together, this is a redox process.

Prove it with oxidation numbers**
In $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ calcium is +2, in $\text{Ca}$ metal it is 0, so the oxidation number falls, confirming reduction. In $\text{I}^{-}$ iodine is -1, in $\text{I}_{2}$ it is 0, so the oxidation number rises, confirming oxidation.

Final answer: $\text{Ca}$ is reduced and $\text{I}$ is oxidised.
Oxidation number of $\text{Ca}$ decreases from +2 in $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to 0 in $\text{Ca}$.
Oxidation number of $\text{I}$ increases from -1 in $\text{I}^{-}$ to 0 in $\text{I}_{2}$.

hints: Think about what solid calcium looks like and what colour iodine vapour is, and what happens to the amount of liquid as it turns into those products.
walkthrough:
Translate the products into what you would see**
Calcium forming at the cathode appears as a grey or silvery metal coating. Iodine liberated at the anode is seen as purple vapour or fumes. As the liquid $\text{CaI}_{2}$ is converted into these products, the volume of melt visibly decreases.
Final answer: Any two: grey / silvery metallic deposit at cathode; purple vapour / gas / fumes at anode; amount of melt decreases.

hints: Calculate the total charge passed from current multiplied by time in seconds, then convert to moles of electrons using $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.
Calculate the moles of iron deposited from the given mass of $1.11\ \text{g}$ and $A_{r} = 55.8$.
Divide moles of electrons by moles of iron to find how many electrons each $\text{Fe}^{n+}$ ion gains, which equals the oxidation number.
walkthrough:
Find the moles of electrons supplied**
Charge is current times time in seconds. For 2 hours at $0.8\ \text{A}$:
$$Q = It = 0.8 \times 2 \times 60 \times 60 = 5760\ \text{C}$$
One mole of electrons carries $96500\ \text{C}$, so:
$$n(\text{e}^{-}) = \frac{5760}{96500} = 0.0597\ \text{mol}$$

Find the moles of iron formed**
Use mass divided by relative atomic mass:
$$n(\text{Fe}) = \frac{1.11}{55.8} = 0.0199\ \text{mol}$$

Use the ratio to get the ion charge**
Each $\text{Fe}^{n+} + n\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}$, so $n$ equals moles of electrons per mole of iron:
$$n = \frac{0.0597}{0.0199} = 3$$
Three moles of electrons make one mole of iron, so the iron ion must be $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and the oxidation number is +3.

Final answer: $Q = 2 \times 60 \times 60 \times 0.8 = 5760\ \text{C}$, moles $\text{e}^{-} = 5760 / 96500 = 0.0597\ \text{mol}$
moles $\text{Fe} = 1.11 / 55.8 = 0.0199\ \text{mol}$
$0.0597 / 0.0199 = 3$, so oxidation number of $\text{Fe} = +3$.
